claim: When the environment changes, vision adapts to maintain accurate perception.
source: When the environment changes, vision adapts to maintain accurate perception.
evidence: This is a general statement about visual adaptation supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Eleven observers wore bright red glasses for five 1-hr periods per day, for 5 days.
source: Eleven observers wore bright red glasses for five 1-hr periods per day, for 5 days.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure conducted in the study.

claim: The world appeared less and less reddish during the 1-hr periods of glasses wear.
source: As expected, the world appeared less and less reddish during the 1-hr periods of glasses wear.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental results.

claim: Across days the world appeared significantly less reddish immediately upon donning the glasses.
source: Critically, across days the world also appeared significantly less reddish immediately upon donning the glasses.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental measurements.

claim: The visual system learned to rapidly adjust to the reddish environment, switching modes to stabilize color vision.
source: These results indicate that the visual system learned to rapidly adjust to the reddish environment, switching modes to stabilize color vision.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results presented in the abstract.

claim: Mode switching likely provides a general strategy to optimize perceptual processes.
source: Mode switching likely provides a general strategy to optimize perceptual processes.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Some visual adaptation processes unfold gradually.
source: Some of the processes producing such adjustments, called visual adaptation, unfold gradually (Clifford et al., 2007; Kohn, 2007; Wark et al., 2007; Webster, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Putting on sunglasses can alter the color of an apple, making it difficult to determine if it is ripe.
source: For example, putting on sunglasses can alter the color of an apple, making it difficult to determine if it is ripe, but as our visual system adapts, the apple's apparent color gradually returns to normal.
evidence: This is an illustrative example based on common knowledge about color perception.

claim: Visual mode switching would aid the many functions that adaptation serves, including improving the detection or discrimination of objects and their properties.
source: Such visual mode switching would aid the many functions that adaptation serves, including improving the detection or discrimination of objects and their properties (Dragoi et al., 2002; Krekelberg et al., 2006; McDermott et al., 2010; Müller et al., 1999; Wissig et al., 2013) and making neural codes more efficient (Seriès et al., 2009; Sharpee et al., 2006; Wainwright, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Visual mode switching makes neural codes more efficient.
source: Such visual mode switching would aid the many functions that adaptation serves, including improving the detection or discrimination of objects and their properties (Dragoi et al., 2002; Krekelberg et al., 2006; McDermott et al., 2010; Müller et al., 1999; Wissig et al., 2013) and making neural codes more efficient (Seriès et al., 2009; Sharpee et al., 2006; Wainwright, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Empirical evidence for learning to switch visual modes is sparse and inconclusive.
source: Empirical evidence for learning to switch visual modes is sparse and inconclusive, however.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the state of prior research in the field.

claim: A few studies have found preliminary support for learning effects on visual adaptation.
source: A few studies have found preliminary support for learning effects on visual adaptation (Engel et al., 2016; Yehezkel et al., 2010), but others have found little to no effect of experience (Tregillus et al., 2016; Vinas et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific prior studies.

claim: Some studies have found little to no effect of experience on visual adaptation.
source: A few studies have found preliminary support for learning effects on visual adaptation (Engel et al., 2016; Yehezkel et al., 2010), but others have found little to no effect of experience (Tregillus et al., 2016; Vinas et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific prior studies.

claim: Previous work has not measured the consequences of moving in and out of an environment multiple times per day over many days.
source: Notably, previous work has not measured the consequences of moving in and out of an environment multiple times per day over many days, and none has tested for changes in the time course of adaptation with experience.
evidence: This is a statement about gaps in prior research based on literature review.

claim: No previous work has tested for changes in the time course of adaptation with experience.
source: Notably, previous work has not measured the consequences of moving in and out of an environment multiple times per day over many days, and none has tested for changes in the time course of adaptation with experience.
evidence: This is a statement about gaps in prior research based on literature review.

claim: The red glasses filter out most of the energy at short wavelengths and maintain most of the energy at long wavelengths.
source: The glasses filter out most of the energy at short wavelengths and maintain most of the energy at long wavelengths.
evidence: This is supported by the transmission spectrum shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The glasses compress the gamut and shift it toward red chromaticity.
source: The glasses compress the gamut and shift it toward red chromaticity.
evidence: This is supported by the monitor gamut data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: One of the main effects of color adaptation is that the dominant color of the environment fades over time.
source: Color adaptation in such situations is relatively well-understood, and one of its main effects is that the dominant color of the environment fades over time (e.g. Belmore and Shevell, 2008; de La Hire, 1694; Eisner and Enoch, 1982; Neitz et al., 2002; von Kries, 1902), restoring the world to its prior, 'normal' appearance.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Observers are highly consistent in their unique yellow judgments.
source: Unique yellow is a commonly used measure in color perception, in part because observers are highly consistent in their judgments (e.g. Brainard et al., 2000; Jameson and Hurvich, 1955; Neitz et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Observers wore the red glasses for five 1-hr periods, each separated by 1 hr without glasses.
source: Observers wore the red glasses for five 1-hr periods, each separated by 1 hr without glasses (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Observers were tested in two sessions on each day, once in the morning and once in the afternoon, for 5 days in a row.
source: On each day, observers were tested in two sessions, once in the morning and once in the afternoon, for 5 days in a row.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: All tests were conducted in a fully lit lab room in order to provide information about the visual environment present.
source: The tests were all conducted in a fully lit lab room in order to provide information about the visual environment present.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions and their rationale.

claim: The world appeared very reddish when observers first put on the glasses.
source: The world appeared very reddish when observers first put on the glasses, and the redness faded over time as vision adapted.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental results.

claim: The redness faded over time as vision adapted.
source: The world appeared very reddish when observers first put on the glasses, and the redness faded over time as vision adapted.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Observers' unique yellow was physically relatively green when they first put on the glasses, which was required to cancel the redness produced by the glasses.
source: The relatively small number (around 220) on the very first test with glasses on (red dots) indicates that observers' unique yellow was physically relatively green, which was required to cancel the redness produced by the glasses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Observers added less green to unique yellow over time, adapting to the red environment during the 1 hr of wearing the glasses.
source: The upward slope of each session's 5 settings shows that observers added less green to unique yellow over time, adapting to the red environment during the 1 hr of wearing the glasses, with the world looking less and less red.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Across days, observers learned to rapidly adjust to the red glasses.
source: Across days, observers learned to rapidly adjust to the red glasses.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study supported by the data.

claim: When observers first put the glasses on, the world appeared less and less reddish across days.
source: That is, when they first put the glasses on, the world appeared less and less reddish.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study supported by the data.

claim: The changes in rapid adjustment were not due to lingering overall adaptation across days.
source: A number of different mechanisms could account for this empirical observation (see Discussion) but the changes were not due to lingering overall adaptation across days, as baseline measurements made before putting the glasses on showed a very different trend (see below).
evidence: This is an inference based on the baseline measurements showing a different trend.

claim: Unique yellow after donning the glasses shifted significantly across days when using observers' averaged settings within only the first 1-min block (t = 6.72, p<0.001).
source: In both cases, unique yellow after donning the glasses again shifted significantly across days (t = 6.72, p<0.001 for the first block; t = 4.11, p<0.01 for the first setting), suggesting observers adjusted to the red glasses relatively quickly (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 2 shows the complete time course of our results as a function of 1-min blocks.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Unique yellow after donning the glasses shifted significantly across days when using observers' very first unique yellow setting in the first block (t = 4.11, p<0.01).
source: In both cases, unique yellow after donning the glasses again shifted significantly across days (t = 6.72, p<0.001 for the first block; t = 4.11, p<0.01 for the first setting), suggesting observers adjusted to the red glasses relatively quickly (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 2 shows the complete time course of our results as a function of 1-min blocks.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The amount of gradual adaptation to the red glasses during the 1 hr of testing did not change across days.
source: The amount of gradual adaptation to the red glasses during the 1 hr of testing, on the other hand, did not change across days.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The grand average slope of unique yellow settings within each 1 hr session was 13.30° of hue angle toward red per hour.
source: The grand average slope was 13.30° of hue angle toward red per hour, and there were no significant changes in slopes across test sessions (ANOVA, F9,100 = 1.06, p=0.40).
evidence: This is a statistical summary of the experimental data.

claim: There were no significant changes in slopes of unique yellow settings across test sessions (ANOVA, F9,100 = 1.06, p=0.40).
source: The grand average slope was 13.30° of hue angle toward red per hour, and there were no significant changes in slopes across test sessions (ANOVA, F9,100 = 1.06, p=0.40).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: About 1 month (36 ± 7 days) after the main experiment, observers returned for a follow-up test.
source: About 1 month (36 ± 7 days) after the main experiment, observers returned for a follow-up test.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Rapid adjustment to the glasses remained strong in the follow-up test; the first test of unique yellow settings was redder than the settings from the first day of the main experiment (t = −4.83, p<0.001).
source: Rapid adjustment to the glasses remained strong; the first test of unique yellow settings was redder than the settings from the first day of the main experiment (t = −4.83, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the follow-up test data.

claim: The follow-up settings were greener than those made on day 5 of the main experiment (t = 3.28, p<0.01).
source: However, the effect was somewhat diminished, as the follow-up settings were greener than those made on day 5 of the main experiment (t = 3.28, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the follow-up test data.

claim: About 66% of the change across the 5 days was maintained in the follow-up test.
source: About 66% of the change across the 5 days was maintained in the follow-up test.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the follow-up test data.

claim: There was a trend for the immediate aftereffect to become less strong across days (all p<0.1 and p>0.05).
source: There was a trend for the immediate aftereffect to become less strong across days, evident in the analyses of the first 5-min test, the first 1-min block, and the first individual match setting (all p<0.1 and p>0.05; Figure 3 green dots show the means of the first 5-min tests).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The decay of the aftereffect followed a roughly exponential shape.
source: The decay followed a roughly exponential shape, as previously reported for color aftereffects (Fairchild and Lennie, 1992; Fairchild and Reniff, 1995; Wright and Parsons, 1934).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data, supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The decay constant of the aftereffect did not change over days (F9,96 = 0.01, p=1).
source: The decay constant, as measured by an exponential fit, did not change over days (F9,96 = 0.01, p=1).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Baseline-corrected results showed a very similar overall pattern across days as the uncorrected data, although some effects became slightly larger.
source: These baseline-corrected results showed a very similar overall pattern across days as the uncorrected data, although some effects became slightly larger (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a comparison of corrected and uncorrected data analyses.

claim: Color constancy is the extent to which objects appear the same color despite changes in viewing conditions.
source: Color constancy, an important benefit of adaptation, is the extent to which objects appear the same color despite changes in viewing conditions (e.g. Brainard and Radonjić, 2014; Foster, 2011; Witzel and Gegenfurtner, 2018).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Color constancy improved across days.
source: Figure 4 plots our results using this metric and shows that color constancy improved across days.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: On the first time observers put on the glasses, they showed about 68% of perfect constancy.
source: The very first time they put on the glasses, observers showed about 68% of perfect constancy, as calculated by the ratio between (1) the Euclidean distance between baseline and the first unique yellow setting with glasses on and (2) the distance between baseline and perfect constancy.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the experimental data.

claim: The amount of color constancy grew significantly as observers learned to immediately adjust to the red glasses (t = 4.60, p<0.001).
source: The amount of constancy grew significantly as observers learned to immediately adjust to the red glasses (t = 4.60, p<0.001), and exceeded 80% on the 5th day.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Color constancy exceeded 80% on the 5th day.
source: The amount of constancy grew significantly as observers learned to immediately adjust to the red glasses (t = 4.60, p<0.001), and exceeded 80% on the 5th day.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Some observers showed a large increase in the amount of rapid adjustment over 5 days, while others demonstrated a flatter pattern.
source: Some observers showed a large increase in the amount of rapid adjustment over 5 days (sample single observer shown in upper panel in Figure 5A, gray circle in Figure 5B), while others demonstrated a flatter pattern (lower panel in Figure 5A, black circle in Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an observation from the individual observer data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The correlation between changes in rapid adjustment from the first day to the fifth day and changes from the first day to the follow-up test was significant (r = 0.81, p=0.003).
source: To test if the individual differences were statistically reliable, we computed the Pearson correlation between the changes in rapid adjustment from the first day to the fifth day, and the changes from the first day to the follow-up test. This correlation was significant (r = 0.81, p=0.003, Figure 5B), indicating that observers who had a larger learning effect over 5 days also retained larger amounts a month later, a form of test-retest reliability.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of individual differences in the data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Individuals appear to differ in their ability to learn to rapidly switch visual modes.
source: Thus, individuals appear to differ in their ability to learn to rapidly switch visual modes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the individual differences observed in the data.

claim: Through experience, observers learned to rapidly adjust to the red glasses, with the world appearing less and less reddish as soon as they put them on.
source: Through experience, observers learned to rapidly adjust to the red glasses, with the world appearing less and less reddish as soon as they put them on.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the experimental data.

claim: Rapid adjustment allows us to compensate for changes in the visual environment.
source: In general, such rapid adjustment allows us to compensate for changes in the visual environment (e.g. Dragoi et al., 2002; Krekelberg et al., 2006; McDermott et al., 2010; Müller et al., 1999; Wissig et al., 2013), while also improving neural coding efficiency (e.g. Seriès et al., 2009; Sharpee et al., 2006; Wainwright, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Rapid adjustment improves neural coding efficiency.
source: In general, such rapid adjustment allows us to compensate for changes in the visual environment (e.g. Dragoi et al., 2002; Krekelberg et al., 2006; McDermott et al., 2010; Müller et al., 1999; Wissig et al., 2013), while also improving neural coding efficiency (e.g. Seriès et al., 2009; Sharpee et al., 2006; Wainwright, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Visual mode switching should enable people to better handle the demands of the complex and changing visual world.
source: Such visual mode switching should enable people to better handle the demands of the complex and changing visual world.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: Color adaptation has a 'fast' and a 'slow' mechanism and involves both receptoral and postreceptoral visual processes.
source: It is well accepted that color adaptation has a 'fast' and a 'slow' mechanism and involves both receptoral and postreceptoral visual processes (e.g. Augenstein and Pugh, 1977; Fairchild and Reniff, 1995; Rinner and Gegenfurtner, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and represents established knowledge.

claim: Through practice a fast adaptation mechanism may have become able to produce stronger and more rapid effects.
source: One plausible interpretation of our results depends on these well-studied mechanisms; it is possible that through practice a fast adaptation mechanism became able to produce stronger and more rapid effects.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results.

claim: Observers who adapted to cylindrical lenses showed fast re-adaptation in a second testing session.
source: For example, observers who adapted to cylindrical lenses, creating a sort of astigmatism, showed fast re-adaptation in a second testing session (Yehezkel et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Clinically astigmatic observers showed little change in adaptation during 6 months following their initial prescription of corrective lenses.
source: However, clinically astigmatic observers showed little change in adaptation during 6 months following their initial prescription of corrective lenses (Vinas et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Adapting to yellow filters produced little change in adaptation across 5 days.
source: Conflicting results also appeared in color perception, where in one study adapting to yellow filters produced little change in adaptation across 5 days (Tregillus et al., 2016), while another report showed that long-term habitual wearers of red and green lenses can adapt more rapidly than naive observers to the color changes the lenses produce (Engel et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Long-term habitual wearers of red and green lenses can adapt more rapidly than naive observers to the color changes the lenses produce.
source: Conflicting results also appeared in color perception, where in one study adapting to yellow filters produced little change in adaptation across 5 days (Tregillus et al., 2016), while another report showed that long-term habitual wearers of red and green lenses can adapt more rapidly than naive observers to the color changes the lenses produce (Engel et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Learning of a visual discrimination task was specific to the visual system's adaptive state, as manipulated by inducing a motion aftereffect.
source: A final bit of evidence for mode switching comes from a different paradigm, in which learning of a visual discrimination task was specific to the visual system's adaptive state, as manipulated by inducing a motion aftereffect (McGovern et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The paradigm in this study differed from past work in that observers adapted to very strong perceptual changes multiple times a day, and the detailed time course of adaptation was tracked in a test setting with rich cues to context.
source: Our paradigm differed from past work in that observers adapted to very strong perceptual changes multiple times a day, and we tracked the detailed time course of adaptation in a test setting with rich cues to context (see below).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design and how it differs from prior work.

claim: Past work on long-term adaptation to colored environments has found that adaptation grows stronger over days.
source: Past work on long-term adaptation to colored environments, for example wearing red glasses or living under red lights continuously for part of the day, has found that adaptation grows stronger over days (Belmore and Shevell, 2008; Belmore and Shevell, 2011; Eisner and Enoch, 1982; Hill and Stevenson, 1976; Kohler, 1963; Neitz et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Past studies on long-term color adaptation did not measure the time course of adaptation, or if observers could learn to rapidly switch between the different viewing conditions.
source: However, these studies did not measure the time course of adaptation, or if observers could learn to rapidly switch between the different viewing conditions.
evidence: This is a statement about gaps in prior research based on literature review.

claim: Past results on long-term color adaptation were highly variable, both within and between studies.
source: These past results were also highly variable, both within and between studies (Belmore and Shevell, 2008; Belmore and Shevell, 2011; Eisner and Enoch, 1982; Eskew and Richters, 2008; Hill and Stevenson, 1976; Kohler, 1963; Neitz et al., 2002; Tregillus et al., 2016), similar to the inconsistency in prior results on mode switching.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: One reason for variability in past results may be that observers were tested with little context present.
source: One reason for this variability may be that observers were tested with little context present.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for variability in prior research.

claim: The test setting in this experiment provided many cues that the visual system could use to tell which environment was present.
source: The test setting in our experiment provided many cues that the visual system could use to tell which environment was present, that is whether the red glasses were on or off.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Context cues may be necessary for mode switching to occur.
source: These context cues may be necessary for mode switching to occur, although precisely which cues are important for which environments remains to be determined.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the experimental design and results.

claim: The baseline unique yellow setting shifted toward physically more greenish across days.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that the baseline unique yellow setting, made immediately prior to the introduction of the red glasses each morning, shifted toward physically more greenish across days.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The shift in baseline was in the opposite direction from the color that the glasses produced and from the shift of the adaptation effect within 1 hr.
source: The shift was in the opposite direction from the color that the glasses produced and from the shift of the adaptation effect within 1 hr.
evidence: This is an observation comparing different aspects of the experimental data.

claim: A similar trend in baseline settings was also found in two previous studies.
source: A similar trend in baseline settings was also found in two previous studies (Engel et al., 2016; Tregillus et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The shift in baseline could be due to the aftereffect following the glasses' removal.
source: While we can only speculate as to the cause of this pattern, it could be due to the aftereffect following the glasses' removal.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the baseline shift.

claim: Long-term adaptation to aftereffects appears to be possible in other domains.
source: Long-term adaptation to aftereffects appears to be possible in other domains (Murch and Hirsch, 1972; Sheth and Shimojo, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The strengthened rapid adaptation substantially improved observers' color constancy.
source: The strengthened rapid adaptation we observed substantially improved observers' color constancy, that is the stability of perceived color despite the changes in viewing conditions (e.g. Brainard and Radonjić, 2014; Foster, 2011; Witzel and Gegenfurtner, 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, with the definition of color constancy supported by citations.

claim: Rapid adaptation, and even faster processes including 'simultaneous' local contrast, are likely major mechanisms that serve color constancy.
source: Rapid adaptation, and even faster processes including 'simultaneous' local contrast, are likely major mechanisms that serve this constancy, (e.g. Rinner and Gegenfurtner, 2000; Smithson and Zaidi, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A current debate in the field is whether constancy is improved for familiar, natural illuminant changes.
source: A current debate in the field is whether constancy is improved for familiar, natural illuminant changes, which our visual systems may have encountered most often (Rüttiger et al., 1999; Delahunt and Brainard, 2004; Pearce et al., 2014; Radonjić and Brainard, 2016; Weiss et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes an ongoing debate in the field, supported by citations to relevant research.

claim: Training with repeated exposure can improve color constancy, at least for a very strong and unfamiliar illumination change.
source: Our results suggest that training with repeated exposure can improve color constancy, at least for a very strong and unfamiliar illumination change.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results.

claim: Observers show some amount of color constancy, and a variety of other perceptual constancies, in most natural settings, without any training.
source: More generally, observers show some amount of color constancy, and a variety of other perceptual constancies, in most natural settings, without any training.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The extent to which perceptual constancies are inborn, determined during development, or learned as an adult remains under investigation.
source: The extent to which these forms of visual mode switching are inborn, determined during development, or learned as an adult remains under investigation (e.g. Jameson and Hurvich, 1989; Sugita, 2004; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes an open question in the field, supported by citations to relevant research.

claim: The aftereffect measured immediately upon removing the red glasses shifted toward the baseline across days.
source: Relatedly, the aftereffect measured immediately upon removing the red glasses shifted toward the baseline across days, implying a faster readjustment to familiar, natural conditions over time.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The trend for aftereffects to shift toward baseline was relatively small and of only modest statistical reliability.
source: However, this trend was relatively small, of only modest statistical reliability, and could be specific to switches from the unnatural red-glasses conditions.
evidence: This is a qualification of the finding about aftereffects.

claim: Adaptation to changes in the dominant color has effects on several sites within the retina.
source: Neurally, adaptation to changes in the dominant color has effects on several sites within the retina (Boynton and Whitten, 1970; Lee et al., 1999; Rieke and Rudd, 2009) as well as cortical stages of color processing (e.g. Engel and Furmanski, 2001; Rinner and Gegenfurtner, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Adaptation to changes in the dominant color has effects on cortical stages of color processing.
source: Neurally, adaptation to changes in the dominant color has effects on several sites within the retina (Boynton and Whitten, 1970; Lee et al., 1999; Rieke and Rudd, 2009) as well as cortical stages of color processing (e.g. Engel and Furmanski, 2001; Rinner and Gegenfurtner, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Behavioral changes across days were not observed in adaptation within the hour of glasses wearing.
source: One hint toward the neural locus of change in our experiment is that behavioral changes across days were not observed in adaptation within the hour of glasses wearing.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The independence of mode switching from classical adaptation suggests that mode switching may arise relatively late in processing.
source: This independence from classical adaptation, which partly arises early in the visual system, suggests that mode switching may arise relatively late in processing (Rinner and Gegenfurtner, 2000).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results, with a citation to support the claim about early adaptation.

claim: Adaptation can be viewed as the result of an inference process, in which the visual system must determine whether the visual environment has changed.
source: Computationally, one can view adaptation as the result of an inference process, in which the visual system must determine whether the visual environment has changed (Grzywacz and de Juan, 2003; Kording et al., 2007; Wark et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Through exposure to the alternating colored and uncolored environment, observers may have learned that the red environment was more likely.
source: Through exposure to the alternating colored and uncolored environment, observers in our experiment may have learned: (1) that the red environment was more likely (i.e. it had higher prior probability); (2) to more efficiently extract evidence of the red environment (giving it a higher likelihood); (3) that the red environment was likely to persist for a long time (making it costly to not adapt); (4) to speed inference by remembering, rather than re-inferring, the past adaptive state for the red environment.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the mechanism of mode switching.

claim: Through exposure to the alternating colored and uncolored environment, observers may have learned to more efficiently extract evidence of the red environment.
source: Through exposure to the alternating colored and uncolored environment, observers in our experiment may have learned: (1) that the red environment was more likely (i.e. it had higher prior probability); (2) to more efficiently extract evidence of the red environment (giving it a higher likelihood); (3) that the red environment was likely to persist for a long time (making it costly to not adapt); (4) to speed inference by remembering, rather than re-inferring, the past adaptive state for the red environment.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the mechanism of mode switching.

claim: Through exposure to the alternating colored and uncolored environment, observers may have learned that the red environment was likely to persist for a long time.
source: Through exposure to the alternating colored and uncolored environment, observers in our experiment may have learned: (1) that the red environment was more likely (i.e. it had higher prior probability); (2) to more efficiently extract evidence of the red environment (giving it a higher likelihood); (3) that the red environment was likely to persist for a long time (making it costly to not adapt); (4) to speed inference by remembering, rather than re-inferring, the past adaptive state for the red environment.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the mechanism of mode switching.

claim: Through exposure to the alternating colored and uncolored environment, observers may have learned to speed inference by remembering, rather than re-inferring, the past adaptive state for the red environment.
source: Through exposure to the alternating colored and uncolored environment, observers in our experiment may have learned: (1) that the red environment was more likely (i.e. it had higher prior probability); (2) to more efficiently extract evidence of the red environment (giving it a higher likelihood); (3) that the red environment was likely to persist for a long time (making it costly to not adapt); (4) to speed inference by remembering, rather than re-inferring, the past adaptive state for the red environment.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the mechanism of mode switching.

claim: Observers may display very different amounts of experimentally measured color constancy, depending upon whether they were asked to make judgments of surface reflectance or of reflected light.
source: Past work has shown that observers may display very different amounts of experimentally measured color constancy, depending upon whether they were asked to make judgments of surface reflectance or of reflected light (Arend and Reeves, 1986; Arend and Goldstein, 1987; Radonjić and Brainard, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Similar rapid re-adaptation has been reported in audition.
source: Mode switching is not limited to color vision. Similar rapid re-adaptation has been reported in audition (Hofman et al., 1998) and sensorimotor paradigms, in which observers adapt to prisms that rotate or displace their visual field (e.g. Redding et al., 2005), or force fields that disturb their motor outcomes (e.g. Wolpert and Flanagan, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Visual mode switching resembles context-dependent learning that arises in conditioning and other memory paradigms.
source: Visual mode switching also resembles context-dependent learning that arises in conditioning and other memory paradigms.
evidence: This is a comparison based on knowledge of different learning paradigms.

claim: Mode switching may be a general solution to the problem of maintaining consistent behavior in a changing world.
source: Mode switching may be a general solution to the problem of maintaining consistent behavior in a changing world.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: All observers had normal color vision, as assessed by the Ishihara Color Blindness Test.
source: All had normal color vision, as assessed by the Ishihara Color Blindness Test, and normal or corrected-to-normal (using contact lenses) visual acuity.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for participants in the study.

claim: None of the observers had worn red glasses for extended periods of time prior to this study.
source: None had worn red glasses for extended periods of time prior to this study.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for participants in the study.

claim: One observer reported that she changed her criterion for unique yellow during the study, and her data showed very large variance in baseline across days, so her data were excluded from further analysis.
source: One of the observers recruited reported that she changed her criterion for unique yellow during the study, and her data showed very large variance in baseline across days. Her data were excluded from further analysis.
evidence: This describes a data exclusion decision made during the analysis.

claim: The glasses transmittance is above 90% at wavelengths over 620 nm.
source: The spectral transmission of the glasses (Figure 1A) shows that the transmittance is above 90% at wavelengths over 620 nm, and less than 10% at wavelengths below 550 nm.
evidence: This is a measurement of the glasses' optical properties shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The glasses transmittance is less than 10% at wavelengths below 550 nm.
source: The spectral transmission of the glasses (Figure 1A) shows that the transmittance is above 90% at wavelengths over 620 nm, and less than 10% at wavelengths below 550 nm.
evidence: This is a measurement of the glasses' optical properties shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The mean luminance of the background office image was 20 candela/m2.
source: The mean luminance of the background office image was 20 candela/m2.
evidence: This describes a parameter of the experimental stimuli.

claim: Observers had 20 s at the most to make one single adjustment.
source: Observers had 20 s at the most to make one single adjustment so that they did not get stuck in making one single setting and did not adapt to the test patch.
evidence: This describes a procedural detail of the experiment.

claim: All settings fell along the nominally iso-luminant plane when not wearing the glasses in order to reduce brightness effects on the judgments.
source: All settings fell along the nominally iso-luminant plane (defined by the LM and S axes, with luminance set to 51 candela/m2) when not wearing the glasses in order to reduce brightness effects on the judgments.
evidence: This describes a design choice in the experimental stimuli.

claim: The stimuli were not adjusted for the glasses, and thus were likely not held at strictly constant luminance or contrast for judgments made while the glasses were on.
source: The stimuli were not adjusted for the glasses, and thus were likely not held at strictly constant luminance or contrast for judgments made while the glasses were on.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the experimental design.
